newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau governor hits back at scolding from China.
newsitem.headline: Macau governor hits back at scolding from China.

text.p: The Governor of Macau has lashed out at China for accusing the Portuguese-ruled gambling enclave of going slow on the transition to Chinese rule and responding too weakly to a wave of violent crime.
General Vasco Rocha Vieira told the Portuguese Lusa news agency in Macau that he would reject "any type of pressure" to speed up the so-called localisation of the civil service.
Macau, a Portuguese enclave for four and a half centuries, reverts to China in 1999, two years after nearby British-ruled Hong Kong is handed back to Beijing.
As part of the run-up to Chinese rule, Macau is gradually to localise its administration, eventually replacing colonial Portuguese officials with local workers.

China's Hong Kong and Macau policy chief Lu Ping said in Beijing on Monday that not enough progress had been made on transition matters, especially localisation of civil servants and the translation of laws from Portuguese into Chinese.

"If these conditions will not improve as soon as possible, this will affect the smooth transfer of power and the political functioning of the Macau Special Administrative Region Government," Lu was quoted as saying in Macau newspapers.
Lu also urged the Macau government to "rectify" the enclave's law and order situation.

Macau has been rocked by a spate of bombings, shootings and firebombings in recent months amid signs of gang warfare between rival triad gangsters vying for protection racket turf in the casinos which form the territory's biggest industry.

Nine people have been murdered so far this year, and Macau police officers, including the senior officer responsible for policing the casino business, have been targeted by firebombers and gun-wielding assasins on motorcycles.
On Thursday night, a Hong Kong businessman was shot dead in a Macau car park by two armed motorcyclists.
General Vieira rejected Lu's criticisms and stressed that the transition was a project requiring joint efforts.
He also said his administration was "more worried than anyone else about the territory's public security situation"
"I think everyone should understand that in a territory like Macau, we need the effective cooperation of all the authorities in the region on this matter," he said.
The traid gangs plaguing Macau are widely believed to have extensive connections in southern China and Hong Kong.
